title: Is This What I Work For?
description:
A brutal month is finally over. Overtime, transit cards, packed lunches — that's not what he's working toward.

Standing outside a convenience store, he checked his phone. Right below the incoming deposit alert: a concert ticket link. His favorite artist. 150,000 won.

"Is it okay to spend this much?"

choices.text: Buy the ticket. Money isn't earned to just sit there.
choices.result_text:
Purchase complete. His balance dipped, but for the first time in a while, he had something to look forward to.

That night at the venue, he screamed himself hoarse.

This is what it feels like to be alive.

choices.text: Hold back. Every 150,000 won matters on the road to 3 billion won.
choices.result_text:
He closed the ticket page.

A mix of pride and emptiness arrived at once. He knows this is the right call — but sometimes, that's the saddest part.

choices.text: Find a cheaper 50,000 won option. YOLO can still compromise.
choices.result_text:
Standing seats on the second floor, far from the stage — but the music was the same.

You don't always get what you want without giving something up. But you don't always have to give everything up either.

title: The Morning After
description:
The morning after the concert, a balance notification was waiting on his phone. Last night's 150,000 won, rendered in cold digits.

His throat was raw and his heart was light, but that number left one corner of it a little heavier. Was this the aftertaste of YOLO?

choices.text: It's fine. Memories are assets too.
choices.result_text:
Not a rationalization — a conclusion.

Sometimes you have to live like this to keep going. The lyrics he screamed last night are still ringing in his ears.

choices.text: Never again. Focus on the goal.
choices.result_text:
He chose regret. A rigorous lesson learned.

But that night — he can't erase it.

title: The Friend Who Said No
description:
Jisoo sipped her coffee and said it plainly.
"I've decided not to get married. For real. Official announcement."

She'd said it before, but this time the tone was different. The look in her eyes was different — relief and freedom, all at once.

"What about you? Do you want to get married?"

choices.text: "Honestly, I'm not sure. Money comes first right now."
choices.result_text:
He said it honestly. Jisoo laughed. "That's the most real answer."

Different choices, no judgment. The kind of conversation that stays with you.

choices.text: "I'm kind of envious. That must not have been an easy decision."
choices.result_text:
He was genuinely envious. The face of someone who has chosen clearly.

Jisoo said, "I'm rooting for you no matter what you pick."

The coffee felt warmer than usual today.

choices.text: "But won't you regret it someday?"
choices.result_text:
Jisoo's expression flickered before she smiled.
"Every time I hear that, I want to ask — what about the people who get married and regret it?"

Fair point. Having your choices questioned is always uncomfortable.

title: Wedding Season Blitz
description:
First week of October. KakaoTalk notifications started before dawn.

Three wedding invitations. Middle school friend, college classmate, work colleague. All in the same month.

Three envelopes. Minimum 50,000 won each, and that's for casual acquaintances.

150,000 won is about to blow away like autumn leaves.

choices.text: Attend all three. Relationships are partly maintained by money.
choices.result_text:
He went to all three. The buffets were good, the dresses were beautiful, and his wallet got lighter.

At this age, 'gift money economics' is its own social system.

choices.text: Go to the close one, send cash to the others.
choices.result_text:
He picked carefully. In person for one real friend — 25,000 won by bank transfer for the other two.

Somewhat guilty, but somewhat less guilty about his bank account.

choices.text: Too broke right now — apologize and skip them.
choices.result_text:
"Sorry, I can't make it — money's tight." Sent.

An awkward silence. But honesty is better. Some relationships might shake — but ones held together only by pretense aren't that solid to begin with.

title: The Question at 35
description:
A call from his mother. "When are you going to get married?"

This question doesn't come only on holidays anymore. At least once a month now. The number 35 seems to have started some kind of countdown in his parents' minds.

"I know someone I could set you up with. Just one meeting."

choices.text: "Now is the time to make money. Marriage comes later." — firm.
choices.result_text:
He said it firmly. His mother went quiet for a moment, then said "okay."

He knows it'll come up again next call, but today, this is enough.

choices.text: "I'll go meet them" — agrees to the blind date.
choices.result_text:
He went. The other person also seemed to have been pushed out the door by their parents.

They exchanged polite pleasantries over coffee and parted. Awkward and a little sad. No text followed.

choices.text: "Mom, I'm struggling right now. Less marriage talk, more encouragement please."
choices.result_text:
For the first time, he said it out loud.

His mother paused, surprised, then: "You're right. I'm sorry. You're doing well."

Sometimes a direct hit is the answer. He felt a little lighter after hanging up.

title: What You Find Living Alone
description:
Sunday night, 11 PM. Eating alone.

He turned on YouTube, then turned it off. Silence.

This stillness — at first lonely — has become comfortable at some point. Nobody critiques how fast he eats. Nobody fights him for the remote.

This freedom is bigger than the loneliness. At least tonight.

choices.text: Embrace the freedom. Alone is enough.
choices.result_text:
Tonight's quiet felt like a gift.

Whether he marries or not — this time is entirely his.
These nights are what shape him.

choices.text: Still lonely though. Wish someone was here.
choices.result_text:
He admitted it honestly. Lonely is lonely.

This loneliness can also be a compass — pointing toward what he truly wants.

choices.text: Call family or a friend.
choices.result_text:
"Hey, what's up?" — that familiar voice.

They talked for twenty minutes about nothing much. After hanging up, the room felt a little less quiet.

title: The Wedding Cost Calculator
description:
Out of boredom, he ran the numbers on marriage costs.

Venue: 15 million won. Honeymoon: 3 million won. Deposit on a place together: 100 million won+. Rings and gifts: 3 million won. First birthday party: 2 million won. Monthly allowance to both sets of parents for 5 years: 36 million won.

Total: 160 million won minimum.

What if he just... invested that instead?

choices.text: Staying single is the rational economic choice — cold conclusion.
choices.result_text:
Numbers don't lie. Marriage is not just an emotional decision — it's a financial one.

The fact that he ran these numbers felt a little bleak, but looking away doesn't change the math.

choices.text: The value of a shared life can't be calculated in money.
choices.result_text:
He closed the calculator.

Life isn't all about ROI. There's something beyond the numbers. He decided to think a little more tonight about what that something is.

choices.text: This should be shared. Friends need to see this.
choices.result_text:
He posted it in the group chat. "Calculated wedding costs btw."

Comments exploded. Half: "Right, it really costs that much." Other half: "Still gotta do it though."

This is our generation's marriage discourse.

title: Anyone for Omakase?
description:
A message in the team chat:
"Got a reservation this Friday for omakase. One seat left. 128,000 won per person. Anyone in?"

Cho Yongmin, associate. Word is he got a big raise after his last job change.

One by one, teammates start replying: "Me!" "Count me in."

choices.text: Go. These moments become professional connections.
choices.result_text:
He went. The food was extraordinary. Over the chef's tasting course explanation, he had his first real conversation with Cho.

These nights build relationships at work. He knows that.

But 128,000 won is 128,000 won.

choices.text: "Maybe next time" — politely bow out.
choices.result_text:
He didn't go. 128,000 won was half his food budget this month.

Watching his colleagues leave on Friday, all excited. A slight outsider feeling — but his account balance survived.

choices.text: "I've never been to omakase — can I ask what kind of food it is?"
choices.result_text:
He admitted he didn't know. Cho actually seemed delighted to explain.

He didn't go this time, but now he knows what it is. Hiding ignorance costs more in the long run.

title: The Omakase Return
description:
A Slack DM from Cho Yongmin:
"That side project we talked about at omakase — want to do it together?"

That seat created this. The 128,000 won looks different now.

choices.text: Join in. I know why this opportunity came.
choices.result_text:
He joined. The project was small — but he got a foot in the door of Cho's network.

The 200,000 won income was secondary. Networks are assets.

choices.text: No bandwidth right now. Politely decline.
choices.result_text:
He declined politely. Cho said "next time."

128,000 won stayed as just a meal. The ROI math stings a little.

title: Other People's Highlights
description:
Opened Instagram absentmindedly before bed.

A classmate was in Bali. A junior bought a new car. Someone at an omakase, someone getting engaged.

{name} swiped through it all in the dark of his room.

Everyone else seemed to have arrived somewhere. Everyone but him.
But he knew — that's their highlight reel, and this is his behind-the-scenes.

choices.text: Delete the app — comparison is a thief
choices.result_text:
Deleted Instagram.

The first few days his hand kept reaching for the empty spot. After a week, sleep came faster.

Not seeing other people's highlights made his own behind-the-scenes feel less shabby.
Quitting comparison was the biggest savings that cost nothing.

choices.text: Keep watching — maybe envy is motivation
choices.result_text:
Scrolled the feed till 2 AM.

'I should get there too.' That resolve was brief, and what remained was emptiness.

Comparison pretends to be motivation, then eats your drive instead.
The next morning, {name} was more tired.

title: The First Luxury Temptation
description:
Department store, first floor. Through the glass, a wallet sat under a spotlight.

800,000 won. More than {name}'s monthly fixed costs.

The clerk held the door open. "Come take a look."

Holding that, for a moment, would feel like becoming someone else.
That 'moment' was the price: 800,000 won.

choices.text: Buy it — my first reward to myself
choices.result_text:
Swiped the card. The shopping bag was heavy.

For a few days it felt good every time I held it. After a month, it was just a wallet.

Luxury's utility peaks at the moment of purchase and drops after.
Still, maybe once, you can buy yourself that moment.

choices.text: Just take a photo and leave — not yet
choices.result_text:
"I'll come back." Walked out of the store.

Riding the escalator down, the wallet kept coming to mind.
But the fact that 800,000 won was still in my account outweighed the regret.

Maybe real luxury is the number you keep by not buying what you wanted.

title: Foreign Car Keys
description:
A friend I hadn't seen in a while plopped his car keys on the table.

A German logo. Couldn't tell if he placed it to be seen, or out of habit.

"It's a lease, just a lease. No big deal." He said it without being asked.

{name} sipped his coffee and smiled. That 'no big deal' was a big deal.

choices.text: Congratulate him sincerely — I have my own pace
choices.result_text:
"Good for you. Enjoy it." He meant it.

There was some envy. But he also knew that car's monthly lease cost more than his own rent.

Not being shaken by others' speed — that was the muscle he'd need most on the way to Gangnam.
He congratulated his friend and walked his own road.

choices.text: It stings — what am I even doing
choices.result_text:
On the subway home, those car keys kept flickering in his mind.

'When will I…' The thought chased its own tail.

Impatience rose. He wanted to swing for the fences.
Comparison is dangerous because it becomes fuel for bad decisions.

title: Staycation Season
description:
Summer. The feed was all hotel pools.

Deluxe room at a 5-star hotel, one night, 350,000 won. Breakfast included. Captioned 'a gift to myself.'

{name} looked at those photos while waiting his turn for the goshiwon's shared shower.

Just one night. The price of a trip to another world.

choices.text: Go for one night — sometimes you need to breathe
choices.result_text:
Check-in. A plush bed, big windows, a clean tub.

For one night, {name} was a different person.

When he returned to the goshiwon the next day, the room looked smaller.
Whether that experience becomes motivation or poison is decided after you come back.

choices.text: There's no tub at home… so just sleep
choices.result_text:
350,000 won was a month of food.

{name} washed up in the shared shower, turned on the fan, and lay down.

Instead of a staycation, he looked at his bank balance. Strangely, it was a comfort.
Spending a different summer from everyone else was also a choice.

title: Do You Play Golf?
description:
The department head asked in passing.

"Kim, you play golf? We're doing a round with a client this weekend."

Golf. Hundreds just to start. Two or three hundred thousand per round.

But he'd heard things get decided on that course.
Between connections that cost money and pride that doesn't.

choices.text: Join in — some things you only see from that table
choices.result_text:
Played clumsily with rented clubs. The ball kept slicing.

But over the five hours of 18 holes, conversations he'd never normally hear went around.
Who's moving where, which deals are coming up.

Golf wasn't a sport, it was a meeting. A pricey ticket, but inside, he saw why.

choices.text: Sit it out — that table isn't my game
choices.result_text:
"I've got no talent for golf, honestly." He waved it off with a smile.

He'll never know what was discussed on that course over the weekend.

Not stepping into the world of connections bought with money — could be a regret, could be a relief.
{name} decided to go his own way. For now.

title: Not Poor, Just Saving
description:
A gathering with friends. Everyone ordered pricey snacks and whiskey.

{name} held out with one cheap beer.

"Why are you such a cheapskate?" someone said, laughing.

The old him would've bristled. But today was different.
He wasn't poor — he was saving. And now he knew it himself.

choices.text: Say it proudly — "I have a goal"
choices.result_text:
"I'm saving up. I've got a goal." {name} said it with a smile.

The table went quiet for a moment. Someone looked sheepish, someone looked envious.

That night he learned frugality isn't shameful — it's proof you have a direction.
It was the night he chose to trust his own numbers over others' eyes.

choices.text: Just laugh it off — no need to explain
choices.result_text:
"Ha, yeah." {name} didn't bother explaining.

He felt no need to. As long as he knew why he was doing this, that was enough.

Slowly finishing his one beer, he thought of the difference he'd keep in his account.
Quiet conviction was the sturdiest conviction of all.
